We're sorry for the stress of seeing what you reported as a duplicate $80 restaurant charge on your credit card. Here is how the billing error process generally works under Regulation Z.

A billing error notice is a written notice that lets the creditor identify your name and account number and, to the extent possible, explains why you believe an error exists, including its type, date, and amount [R-1026.13#1]. It must be received no later than 60 days after the first periodic statement reflecting the alleged error was sent [R-1026.13#1]. We don't yet know your dates, so we can't say whether your notice falls within that window, and the sources don't tell us how notices outside it are handled.

After a creditor receives a billing error notice, it must send written acknowledgment within 30 days unless it has already resolved the matter. It must complete the resolution procedures within 2 complete billing cycles, and no later than 90 days [R-1026.13#1]. While a dispute is pending, you need not pay the disputed amount, and the creditor may not try to collect it [R-1026.13#2]. It also may not make an adverse credit report because you did not pay that amount [R-1026.13#2]. The creditor may still collect any undisputed portion [R-1026.13#2].

If the creditor determines a billing error occurred as asserted, it must correct the error, credit the disputed amount, and send a correction notice [R-1026.13#2]. If it determines no error occurred after a reasonable investigation, it must send an explanation and, if you ask, copies of documentary evidence [R-1026.13#2].
